papers.abstract: Chordoma is a rare, locally aggressive bone tumor of the skull base, mobile spine, and sacrum that requires complex surgery, specialized radiation, and multidisciplinary surveillance. Centralizing care at high-volume, academic, or specialized centers may improve outcomes by concentrating expertise, but may also introduce access barriers. We systematically reviewed reported associations between centralized care and surgical, perioperative, treatment-related, and oncologic outcomes in chordoma. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines and searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception through November 5, 2026. Included studies evaluated chordoma patients and a centralization-related exposure, such as facility volume, academic status, or facility type. Where chordoma-specific data were not reported, authors were contacted and unadjusted chordoma-specific estimates were derived from patient-level data. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, and findings were synthesized narratively. Of 1,790 records, 5 retrospective US registry studies met inclusion criteria. Centralization definitions varied across facility volume, academic status, and type. Centralized care was generally associated with greater surgery use and improved overall survival; surgery was more common at high-volume facilities (97.3% vs. 73.7%), and adjusted hazard ratios for worse survival at lower-volume or nonacademic centers ranged from 1.7 to 2.5 (derived from two non-overlapping cohorts). Patients at centralized centers traveled farther and were more often younger, privately insured, or metropolitan residents. High-volume and academic treatment settings were generally associated with longer survival in chordoma, supporting further study of specialized multidisciplinary care, though this advantage is inseparable from the access barriers shaping who reaches them. The registry evidence is limited by overlapping cohorts, differing definitions, and residual confounding, so it cannot establish the effect of referral or an optimal volume threshold. Future studies should adopt standardized measures of care setting and examine oncologic outcomes and access-related tradeoffs to inform models of care that can improve survival while minimizing disparities.

papers.abstract: Minibeam radiation therapy (MBRT) preserves normal tissue while maintaining antitumour efficacy, yet the mechanisms underlying this remarkable normal tissue tolerance remain poorly understood. Although adaptive immune responses have been implicated in the antitumour effects of spatially fractionated radiotherapy, their contribution to normal tissue preservation remains unknown. Here, we used a loss-of-function model to determine whether mature T cells are required for the expression of the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype associated with MBRT. Immunocompetent Fischer 344 rats and athymic nude rats received X-ray MBRT or conventional radiotherapy (CRT) at a mean dose of 30 Gy and were followed for up to six months. Long-term normal tissue response was assessed using complementary behavioural analyses, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and histopathological evaluation of immune infiltration, vascular integrity, glial activation and neuronal survival. Nude rats developed beam-path alopecia and skin lesions earlier than immunocompetent rats and showed a transient reduction in cortical CD31 staining at 7 days post-irradiation, indicating greater acute radiosensitivity without mature T cells. Beyond this early window, the long-term phenotype was comparable between strains: no MRI-detectable lesions, no neuronal loss and no sustained glial activation at 6 months. MBRT induced modest late reductions in exploratory behaviour and recognition memory in both strains, with no significant strain × irradiation interaction. Histologically, MBRT elicited a moderate and transient CD3+ T-cell infiltration that resolved within seven days, whereas CRT induced a stronger and more sustained inflammatory response. Mature T cells modulate the acute tissue reaction to MBRT but are not required for the long-term normal tissue-sparing phenotype. Within the sensitivity of this study, powered for large effects only, mature T cells are unlikely to be a major determinant of long-term MBRT tissue preservation, redirecting attention towards innate immune, vascular and stromal processes.

papers.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) affects millions globally, causing significant lifelong morbidity and early death. As childhood mortality is reduced and SCD patients are surviving to adulthood, increased risk of hematological malignancy (HM) is becoming evident. Risk of therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)/acute myeloid leukemia, following gene therapy or hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is also higher in SCD. The specific pathobiology that predisposes to HM is necessary to address, since survival has improved and gene therapy and HSCT are being increasingly used. We modelled the increased risk of HM in humanized SCD mice, compared to age-, sex- and strain-matched normal counterparts. We serially monitored hematopoiesis in blood and bone marrow up to 1-year-of-age and performed highly sensitive, error-corrected deep sequencing of 450 MDS/HM-associated genes. Unlike controls, SCD mice showed an 'ageing-like' phenotype with premature development of myeloid-biased hematopoiesis and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) mutational profile characteristic of aged mice/humans. Furthermore, a high proportion of SCD mice developed hematopoiesis with dysplastic features reminiscent of MDS morphology and higher clonal hematopoiesis burden. Imposition of regenerative stress by serial HSCT further increased HSPC mutational burden, resulting in evolution/expansion of clones harboring oncogenic driver mutations. Our study indicates that increased HSC regenerative stress, imposed either by chronic erythropoietic demand or via autologous HSCT in SCD increases the risk of developing clonal hematopoiesis and MDS-like features. Our study provides insights into a mechanism underlying increased risk of HM in this non-malignant hematological disorder, and suggests that early intervention with curative therapies may circumvent this risk.

papers.abstract: In the phase 2 FORTE trial, transplant-eligible newly diagnosed multiple myeloma patients aged ≤65 years were randomized to (R1) carfilzomib-lenalidomide-dexamethasone followed by autologous stem cell transplantation (KRd-ASCT), twelve cycles of KRd (KRd12), or carfilzomib-cyclophosphamide-dexamethasone followed by ASCT (KCd-ASCT). Eligible patients were then randomized (R2) to maintenance with carfilzomib for 2 years plus lenalidomide until progression (KR) or lenalidomide alone until progression (R). With extended follow-up (median 99 months from R1 and 85 months from R2), KRd-ASCT significantly increased progression-free survival (PFS, median 98 months) versus KRd12 (median 70 months; HR 0.71, p=0.027) and KCd-ASCT (median 67 months; HR 0.66, p=0.006). A significant benefit in PFS2 was also observed versus both KRd12 (HR 0.65, p=0.02) and KCd-ASCT (HR 0.68, p=0.04) and in terms of overall survival (OS) versus KCd-ASCT (8-year OS: 76% vs 68%; HR 0.65, p=0.04). KR maintenance significantly improved PFS versus R (HR 0.67, p=0.02), with a time-dependent effect persisting up to two years after carfilzomib discontinuation; no differences in PFS2/OS were observed. KR significantly increased rate of measurable residual disease (MRD) conversion (sHR 0.47, p=0.03) during active treatment, and reduced MRD resurgence (sHR 0.53, p=0.001) versus R. Median duration of MRD negativity was 50.5 months in KR vs. 38 months in R arm. MRD-negative patients had significantly prolonged PFS with KR (HR 0.60, p=0.031); MRD-positive patients benefited from KR mainly during carfilzomib therapy (HR 0.46, p=0.05). The cumulative incidence of second primary malignancies was 6%. In conclusion, long-term follow-up confirms the high effectiveness of KRd-ASCT and KR maintenance. NCT02203643.

papers.abstract: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) involvement is commonly considered a contraindication to surgical resection in locally advanced pancreatic cancer. The role of SMA resection during pancreatectomy remains controversial, with historical data suggesting prohibitive morbidity and poor survival. A systematic search of the literature was performed. Studies reporting on patients undergoing pancreatectomy with concomitant SMA resection were included. Primary endpoints were perioperative morbidity, 90-day mortality, and survival. Additional data on neoadjuvant treatment, patient selection, anticoagulation, reconstruction techniques, and oncological outcomes were also extracted. In total, 12 studies reporting on 320 patients undergoing pancreatectomy with SMA resection were included. All included studies showed a serious risk of bias and described highly selected patients. Concomitant venous resection was performed in 97% (n = 244/252) of patients and a total pancreatectomy in 63% (n = 173/275). Arterial reconstruction was achieved by graft interposition in 48% (n = 128/269), primary end-to-end anastomosis in 39% (n = 106/269), and splenic artery transposition in 13% (n = 34/269) of patients. Major morbidity and 90-day mortality were 31% (n = 88/284) and 8% (n = 27/320), respectively. Complications included post-pancreatectomy hemorrhage in 19% (n = 39/202) of patients and mesenteric ischemia in 3% (n = 6/202). R0 resection was achieved in 80% (n = 136/171) of patients. Median reported survival from surgery ranged from 8 to 20 months. The highest reported 5-year survival was 21%. Pancreatectomy with SMA resection is associated with specific perioperative morbidity and an 8% mortality rate. Since these outcomes were achieved by expert groups under highly selected circumstances, only implementation at high-volume centers with dedicated vascular pancreatic surgery expertise should be considered.

papers.abstract: Neuroblastoma is the most frequent extracranial solid tumor in children and the main cause of early childhood cancer deaths. Relapse occurs in more than half of high-risk patients despite rigorous multimodal therapy, and four-year overall survival in relapsed disease is approximately 20%. Anti-GD2 monoclonal antibodies and GD2-directed CAR T cell treatment have advanced the field, although neither has eliminated neuroblastoma's immune resistance. Current immunotherapy has three interrelated challenges. GD2 heterogeneity lets antigen-negative subclones escape and cause recurrence. Inhibitory cytokines, regulatory T cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells dominate the TME. MHC class I downregulation frequently renders traditional αβ T cell methods ineffective, even with the target antigen present. Gamma-delta (γδ) T cells offer a distinct mechanism. They recognize tumor targets without antigen presentation by sensing stress-induced ligands through NKG2D and DNAM-1 and phosphoantigens through butyrophilin proteins BTN3A1 and BTN2A1. This recognition holds regardless of MHC class I status. In conjunction with anti-GD2 antibodies, CD16 expression boosts antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In neuroblastoma lesions, γδ T cells are the primary antitumoral fraction in tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte products, indicating compatibility with the disease's immune system. This study examines neuroblastoma immunotherapy failure mechanisms and innovative γδ T cell platforms, such as non-engineered allogeneic products, composite γδ T plus NK cell techniques, and CAR- and AbTCR-modified designs. A biomarker-driven patient selection paradigm and product standardization, in vivo persistence, and TME suppression are examined. NCT05400603, the first trial of adoptive transfer of ex vivo-expanded allogeneic γδ T cells in a population that includes pediatric neuroblastoma patients, is crucial for proving the mechanism.

papers.abstract: Chlorogenic acid (CGA), a naturally occurring polyphenol abundant in coffee and tea, has demonstrated antitumor activity in multiple experimental models. However, the cellular targets and mechanisms of CGA remain incompletely understood. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) are key immunosuppressive components of the tumor microenvironment. Here, we investigated whether CGA regulates MDSC ferroptosis, thereby influencing tumor progression and antitumor immunity. We established MDSC-conditioned medium systems using tumor cells or CD8⁺ T cells as responder cells and evaluated the effects of CGA in murine models of lung cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma. Our results showed that CGA protected MDSCs from ferroptosis and reduced ferroptosis-associated lipid peroxidation. Consequently, conditioned medium derived from CGA-treated MDSCs showed a reduced capacity to promote tumor cell proliferation and migration and was less effective at suppressing CD8⁺ T cell function. In vivo, CGA significantly suppressed tumor growth in murine models of lung cancer and hepatocellular carcinoma and reduced the expression of MDSC-associated immunosuppressive factors within tumors. Flow cytometric analysis further revealed a lower proportion of BODIPY-positive cells among tumor-infiltrating CD11b⁺GR-1⁺ MDSCs in CGA-treated mice. CGA treatment also enhanced intratumoral CD8⁺ T cell responses. Mechanistically, CGA promoted NRF2 nuclear accumulation and increased GPX4 expression in MDSCs. NRF2 knockdown abolished the protective effect of CGA against MDSC ferroptosis. Together, these findings indicate that CGA restrains tumor progression, at least in part, by modulating MDSC ferroptosis through an NRF2-dependent mechanism. Collectively, these data identify MDSCs as a potential cellular target of CGA and support further evaluation of CGA as an immunomodulatory anticancer agent.

papers.abstract: Gastric cancer progression is closely linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling and changes in the tumour microenvironment, yet biomarkers capturing these coordinated processes remain limited. We integrated transcriptomic datasets, machine-learning-based prioritisation, multi-cohort validation, single-cell analysis and functional assays to investigate ADAMTS2. ADAMTS2 was consistently upregulated in gastric cancer tissues and cell lines and discriminated tumour from normal tissue with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.945. Higher ADAMTS2 expression was associated with advanced clinicopathological features and poorer survival. Genome-wide co-expression and weighted gene co-expression network analyses identified an ADAMTS2-associated module strongly linked to EMT, TGF-β activity and invasion. These associations were consistently reproduced across three independent gastric cancer cohorts, with increasing ADAMTS2 expression accompanied by enhanced mesenchymal and invasion-related programmes and an opposing epithelial pattern. Single-cell analysis localised ADAMTS2 predominantly to fibroblast and myofibroblast populations. Across three cohorts, ADAMTS2 correlated positively with stromal and immune scores and inversely with tumour purity, while multi-algorithm deconvolution revealed concordant associations with fibroblast/CAF, macrophage and endothelial-cell infiltration. In AGS and HGC-27 cells, ADAMTS2 knockdown suppressed proliferation, colony formation, migration and invasion, increased E-cadherin, and decreased N-cadherin and vimentin. Stable knockdown also reduced xenograft growth. Collectively, these findings identify ADAMTS2 as a candidate biomarker connecting an EMT- and ECM-remodelling transcriptional programme with a fibroblast-rich, immune-remodelled microenvironment in gastric cancer.

papers.abstract: BRAF V600E-mutant colorectal cancer (CRC) has aggressive behavior and limited therapeutic options. We investigated whether dual-specificity phosphatase 4 (DUSP4) contributes to this phenotype and defined its molecular mechanism. DepMap and GEO data were integrated to nominate BRAF V600E-selective candidates. DUSP4 expression was validated in 30 paired tumors/normal tissues and an independent cohort (n = 326). Gain/loss-of-function studies were performed in HT29/RKO cells and xenografts. IP-MS, co‑IP, immunofluorescence, cycloheximide chase, inhibitor assays, and ubiquitination assays defined the mechanism. CD8+ T cells were analyzed by flow cytometry and chemokines by ELISA. DUSP4 was preferentially expressed in BRAF V600E‑mutant CRC and associated with nodal (P = 0.005) and distant metastasis (P = 0.019), and shorter overall survival. High DUSP4 independently predicted mortality [HR=2.102, 95%CI 1.395-3.165, P < 0.001]. Overexpression promoted proliferation, migration, and xenograft growth; knockdown produced opposite effects. Mechanistically, DUSP4 reduced PTEN protein stability and activated PI3K-AKT. DUSP4 recruited E3 ligase TRIM27, promoting K48‑linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of PTEN. TRIM27 manipulation partially rescued DUSP4‑dependent phenotypes. In vitro, DUSP4-overexpressing CRC cells impaired CD8+ T cell function, as evidenced by decreased expression of IFN-γ, GZMB, and CD107a. DUSP4 overexpression was associated with downregulated CXCL9/16, IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2, and upregulated IL-10, effects partially reversed by PTEN overexpression. DUSP4 is preferentially expressed in BRAF V600E-mutant CRC and independently predicts poor prognosis. It promotes tumor progression via a novel TRIM27-PTEN-PI3K-AKT axis, and modulates the immune microenvironment by impairing CD8+ T cell function. DUSP4 may serve as a candidate prognostic biomarker and warrants further investigation as a potential therapeutic target.

papers.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome driven by advanced malignancies and is closely linked to poor treatment tolerance and unfavorable prognosis. The neural-tumor-immune crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment is increasingly recognized as a key determinant of cachexia progression. Here, we show that gastric cancer (GC) patients with chronic stress (CS) exhibit poor outcomes that are closely associated with advanced N stage, perineural invasion, and cachexia. In vivo, CS accelerates GC growth and induces cachectic phenotypes, including gastrocnemius loosening, myofiber atrophy, and epididymal white adipose atrophy with browning. Mechanistically, CS enhances neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) formation and promotes sustained release of NETs-derived DNA, which drives both tumor progression and systemic metabolic wasting. NETs-DNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that persistently activates the cGAS-STING/NLRP3 inflammasome signaling axis in macrophages in a time-dependent manner, leading to amplified inflammatory responses that promote myocyte atrophy and impair lipid droplet formation. In parallel, CS strengthens neuro-tumor communication; nociceptive neurons sustain NETs formation via a feedforward CGRP-NGF signaling loop, whereas gastric vagotomy attenuates CS-induced NETs formation and consequently suppresses both tumor progression and cachexia. Importantly, combined inhibition of the CGRP/RAMP1 axis and the cGAS-STING/NLRP3 pathway produces synergistic suppression of GC growth and cachectic phenotypes. Collectively, these findings identify a stress-neuro-immune circuit that drives GC progression and cachexia, and highlight the CGRP/RAMP1 and cGAS-STING/NLRP3 axes as potential therapeutic targets.

papers.abstract: Venous congestion is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of organ dysfunction during acute kidney injury requiring continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Although the Venous Excess Ultrasound (VExUS) score is a promising bedside marker of systemic venous congestion, its dynamic evolution during CRRT remains unknown. We aimed to describe serial changes in VExUS during CRRT and explore their association with ultrafiltration intensity and fluid balance. MAVERIC was a prospective single-centre observational pilot study including adults undergoing CRRT for acute kidney injury. VExUS was assessed before CRRT initiation and after 24 and 48 hours. The primary objective was to describe temporal changes in VExUS using an alluvial plot. Patients were classified into three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution. Associations with net ultrafiltration (NUF) and cumulative fluid balance were explored. Forty-seven patients were included. Overall, VExUS grades decreased significantly during the first 48 hours of CRRT (p = 0.0048). Three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution were identified: persistently low congestion (45%, n = 21), resolving congestion (32%, n = 15), and persistent or worsening congestion (23%, n = 11). Patients with resolving congestion had the highest NUF rates (1.35 [0.85-1.66] mL/kg/h) and the most negative cumulative fluid balance (-36.7 [-74.6 to -21.1] mL/kg), with significant differences across groups (p = 0.003 and p < 0.001, respectively). Patients with persistent or worsening congestion had lower NUF rates. Serial VExUS assessment provides dynamic information on systemic venous congestion during CRRT. Three a priori-defined patterns of congestion evolution were associated with differences in net ultrafiltration and fluid balance. Serial VExUS monitoring may help identify patients with persistent or worsening congestion, raising the hypothesis that it could inform reassessment of decongestion strategies. Whether integrating serial VExUS assessment into individualised decongestive strategies improves renal outcomes should be evaluated in prospective interventional studies.

papers.abstract: Intra-abdominal candidiasis is frequent in critically ill surgical patients and is associated with high mortality. Whether empiric antifungal therapy improves outcomes after surgery for intra-abdominal infection (IAI) in critically ill patients remains uncertain. We conducted a retrospective single-center data warehouse-based cohort study of 1,061 adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) after surgery for IAI between 2018 and 2024. Patients who received systemic antifungal therapy within 24 hours after surgery were compared with those who did not. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were day-5 renal dysfunction, assessed by the renal SOFA component and the creatinine-based KDIGO stage, and the need for surgical reintervention. Adjusted analyses used propensity-score overlap weighting. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses used a Peritonitis Score ≥3, the identification of at least one organism in peritoneal samples, and a yeast-positive peritoneal sample. Empiric antifungal therapy was initiated in 46.0% of patients. Peritoneal sampling was available in 957 patients (90.2%); 21.4% had no organism identified and 25.2% had a yeast-positive sample. In adjusted analyses, empiric therapy was not associated with reduced 30-day mortality (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.83-2.78), lower day-5 renal SOFA score, lower KDIGO stage, or fewer reinterventions. Findings were consistent in patients with Peritonitis Score ≥3, with at least one identified organism, and with a yeast-positive sample. ICU and hospital stays were longer in treated patients after weighting. Empiric antifungal therapy initiated within 24 hours after surgery for severe IAI was not associated with improved short-term outcomes. NA.

papers.abstract: For decades, ambulatory anesthesia pathways have commonly required a "responsible adult" before discharge after sedation or anesthesia. In practice, this requirement may function as a binary eligibility criterion based on a patient's social circumstances. However, the empirical evidence evaluating discharge without an escort remains limited and derives largely from observational studies. This Focal Point argues that carefully selected low-risk patients should be studied within structured alternative discharge pathways that preserve safe transportation, communication, observation, and rescue capacity. Such pathways should not permit self-driving or unrestricted solo discharge. The aim is to determine whether postanesthesia safeguards can be matched more precisely to patient, anesthetic, procedural, recovery, transport, and postdischarge risk while preserving conventional adult support for patients whose clinical circumstances warrant it.

papers.abstract: Proprietary processed EEG indices are less accurate in young children. We evaluated spectral edge frequency 95 (SEF95), a nonproprietary EEG index representing the frequency below which 95% of total EEG power resides, to establish target thresholds for varying anaesthetic depths during propofol anaesthesia in toddlers. Secondary objectives were to assess the relationship between SEF95 and plasma propofol concentration, and to evaluate airway reactivity during laryngoscopy. In this prospective study of toddlers aged 13 to 24 months, Dixon's up-and-down method and centred isotonic regression were used to determine the SEF95 targets for 50% (ED50) and 90% (ED90) probability of nonresponse to three clinical stimuli: pacifier placement (assessing consciousness), electrical nerve stimulation (nociception), and laryngoscopy (intubation readiness). Linear mixed-effects regression was used to analyse the association between plasma propofol concentration and SEF95. Among 51 toddlers, SEF95 ED50 and ED90 targets (Hz) were 21.8 (90% CI 20.8-23.4) and 20.3 (19.1-20.7) Hz for pacifier placement, 12.0 (10.8-18.3) and 10.4 (8.7-11.3) Hz for electrical stimulation, and 10.3 (4.6-11.8) and 4.4 (1.5-5.4) Hz for laryngoscopy. Each 1 Hz increase in SEF95 corresponded to a 0.21 μg ml-1 decrease in plasma propofol (r=0.46, P<0.001), as described by the equation: plasma propofol concentration (μg ml-1)=5.80-0.21×SEF95 (Hz). This study defined EEG SEF95 targets for loss of consciousness, response to noxious stimuli, and intubation readiness in toddlers aged 13 to 24 months. When combined with existing infant data, these age-specific SEF95 targets can optimise propofol titration and dosing accuracy during EEG-guided propofol anaesthesia in patients aged <2 yr. papers.abstract: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring commonly uses acceleromyography (AMG) or electromyography (EMG). Acceleromyography requires unrestricted thumb movement, whereas EMG is independent of thumb motion. We compared the accuracy and precision of AMG and EMG responses after patients' arms were immobilized during routine surgical positioning. Patients undergoing general anaesthesia without neuromuscular block were enrolled. EMG and AMG monitors were placed on contralateral arms, and both arms were tucked under surgical drapes. The monitors simultaneously recorded train-of-four ratio (TOFR) after ulnar nerve stimulation every minute. Accuracy was defined as TOFR variability from the expected baseline value (1.00), and precision as consistency of repeated measurements, quantified by the coefficient of repeatability (CR). Failed measurements were defined as the absence of valid quantitative TOFR values, displayed as "0" or "?". AMG TOFR values were normalized to patient-specific baseline TOFR measurements for secondary analyses. Forty patients provided 3,733 TOFR measurements (1,879 EMG and 1,854 AMG). EMG was more accurate than AMG (mean EMG-AMG difference in absolute deviation from 1.0, -0.108; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.134 to -0.083; p < 0.001) and more precise, with a smaller CR (0.10 vs. 0.35; p < 0.001), including compared with normalized AMG (CR, 0.35). Device failure rate was lower with EMG than AMG (3.6% vs. 27.7%; p = 0.0003). Failures increased over time, particularly for AMG after approximately 45 minutes. EMG provided more accurate and precise TOFR measurements than AMG, including normalized AMG, with fewer failures, supporting EMG-based monitoring when upper extremity mobility is restricted. papers.abstract: Uncertainty remains regarding the clinical advantages of sugammadex over neostigmine in older adults, particularly for recovery efficiency and postoperative outcomes. To compare the effects of sugammadex versus neostigmine on postoperative recovery and clinical outcomes in adults aged 60 years and older undergoing surgery. This systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized controlled trials. The primary outcome was postoperative residual neuromuscular blockade (PRNB). Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, hospital length of stay, time to extubation, hypoxemia, pneumonia, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Effect measures were risk ratio and mean difference. A total of 851 participants were included, and 50.2% received sugammadex. Sugammadex was associated with a lower risk of PRNB (RR 0.34 [95% CI: 0.18; 0.64]; p < 0.001; I² = 54%), with moderate between-study heterogeneity; however, the 95% prediction interval (0.11; 1.03) included the null value. Sugammadex significantly reduced PACU length of stay (MD -8.84 [95% CI: -12.18; -5.51], p < 0.001, I2 = 0%), hospital length of stay (MD -1.12 [95% CI: -2.01; -0.24], p < 0.01, I2 = 16%), and hypoxemia (RR = 0.61 [95% CI: 0.38; 0.97]; p = 0.04, I2 = 0%). No statistically significant differences were observed for the remaining outcomes. Sugammadex was associated with a lower risk of PRNB and shorter PACU stays compared with neostigmine. Although the primary analyses suggested reductions in hypoxemia and hospital length of stay, these associations were not statistically significant after the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. papers.abstract: European product information does not recommend sugammadex in severe renal impairment, including dialysis, because renal elimination is markedly reduced. European data describing reversal practice in this population are limited. To determine whether sugammadex was the predominant pharmacological reversal agent among patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis. This secondary analysis of the prospective DELPO cohort included adults who received general anaesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, and pharmacological reversal with sugammadex or neostigmine at 43 Spanish hospitals. Patients were classified as being in GFR categories G1-G3 (eGFR ≥30 mL min-¹ 1.73 m-²) or GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis (eGFR <30 mL min-¹ 1.73 m-² or dialysis). Reversal-agent use was described overall and according to renal function. The analysis included 1331 patients, of whom 35 were in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis, including 20 receiving dialysis. Sugammadex was used in 1,278 of 1,331 patients overall (96.0%), in 1248 of 1,296 patients in GFR categories G1-G3 (96.3%), and in 30 of 35 patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis (85.7%; 95% CI, 70.6-93.7%). Among the 20 patients receiving dialysis, sugammadex was administered to 16 (80.0%; 95% CI, 58.4-91.9%). Among patients in GFR categories G4-G5 or receiving dialysis who received pharmacological reversal, sugammadex was used in 85.7% (30/35), including 80.0% (16/20) of patients receiving dialysis, despite current European product information not recommending its use in this population.

papers.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is defined by clinical and radiographic criteria, yet patients differ in underlying biology, physiological impairment, and regional lung injury. Such heterogeneity may influence treatment response. Current ventilatory strategies, however, are generally guided by physiological targets without fully accounting for the biological, structural, and functional diversity of ARDS. Computed tomography, lung ultrasound, and electrical impedance tomography offer complementary information on lung morphology, aeration, and regional ventilation, while selected approaches may inform recruitability assessment. Nevertheless, evidence that imaging-defined subphenotypes identify patients who derive differential clinical benefit from specific interventions remains limited. This review examines the contribution of lung imaging to individualized respiratory management in ARDS, separating descriptive and prognostic findings from evidence of treatment-effect modification. Limitations of categorical classification and the dynamic nature of lung injury are discussed alongside the potential integration of imaging, physiological, biological, and clinical data. Such multimodal approaches remain investigational but may support evaluation of heterogeneous responses to positive end-expiratory pressure, prone positioning, and other supportive strategies. Before these approaches can guide treatment selection, standardized image acquisition, reproducible classification, longitudinal assessment, independent validation, and prospective demonstration of clinical benefit are required.

papers.abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) importantly contribute to postoperative morbidity and mortality, particularly for patients classified American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status III. Whether PPC risk factors depend on sex remains unclear. We hypothesize that sex modifies the relationship between perioperative risk factors and PPCs in patients assigned an ASA III status undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia. We performed a secondary analysis of prospective data from 1,202 patients undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery. We collected data on preoperative patient demographics, comorbidities, intraoperative physiology, medications, and procedure information. The primary outcome was a composite of PPCs by postoperative day 7. Mixed-effects linear models incorporated sex as main and interaction effect. Age, upper abdominal surgery, and surgical duration significantly increased the odds of ≥ 1 PPC by postoperative day 7. Male patients presented a higher rate of ≥ 3 PPCs, and female patients received higher tidal volumes per predicted body weight and driving pressures. Sex did not significantly modify the relationship between perioperative factors and the primary outcome (no P < 0.05 for the interaction with sex). In the secondary analysis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) affected atelectasis more strongly in male than in female patients (relative odds ratio for female vs male patients, 0.27; 95% confidence interval, 0.13 to 0.57). In patients classified ASA III undergoing noncardiothoracic surgery with general anesthesia, perioperative factors are predominantly not modified by sex in their relationship to PPCs. The association between GERD and atelectasis in male patients could be explored in future prospective studies as a target for reducing PPCs.

papers.abstract: We sought to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis with the primary objective to identify prognostic factors associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Our secondary objective was to report the incidence of this entity. We searched, MEDLINE® and Embase® from inception through 4 May 2024 for all studies in patients with critical illness that reported catheter-related thrombosis, with an updated search performed on 23 October 2025. We included English-language studies that described prognostic factors for developing a catheter-related thrombosis or reported the incidence of this complication in the critical care setting. Two authors performed citation screening and data extraction. We pooled adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) separately for prognostic factors using a random-effects model and inverse variance weighting. Risk of bias for individual studies was evaluated using the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool. We assessed certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations approach. We included 32 studies involving 11,943 patients. Identified prognostic variables with a moderate- or high-certainty association for developing a catheter-related thrombosis include increasing age (aOR per 10-yr increase, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06 to 1.27; three studies; 1,594 patients; high certainty), trauma-related admission (aOR, 1.48; 95% CI, 0.93 to 2.34; three studies; 3,089 patients; high certainty), surgical-related admission (aOR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.77 to 3.52; three studies; 2,208 patients; aHR, 1.35; 95% CI, 0.60 to 3.02; two studies; 297 patients; high certainty), internal jugular insertion site as compared with other insertion sites (aOR, 3.76; 95% CI, 2.82 to 5.01; four studies; 4,681 patients; high certainty), single/double-lumen as compared with more lumens (aOR, 1.61; 95% CI, 0.82 to 3.13; three studies; 1,594 patients; moderate certainty), and peripheral insertion site (aOR, 2.30; 95% CI, 0.74 to 7.08; two studies; 264 patients; moderate certainty). The median incidence of catheter-related thrombosis was 13.3% [interquartile range, 3.7%-31.3%]. In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we found that increasing age, surgical type admissions, large catheters, and factors potentially related with catheter duration were associated with developing a catheter-related thrombosis in the critical care setting. Furthermore, we identified significant variation in the reported rates of catheter-related thrombosis, with an average rate of approximately 1 in every 8 patients. When these identified risk factors are present, clinicians may consider more aggressive thromboprophylaxis regimens to better tailor prevention strategies to individual patient risk profiles. papers.abstract: Microaxial flow pumps (mAFP) improve hemodynamics and outcomes in myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (CS) but are associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT). We aimed to determine the incidence and factors associated with RRT and evaluate its association with mortality in a real-world cohort of miscellaneous CS patients supported with mAFP. We conducted a retrospective multicentre registry including CS patients supported with mAFP across 11 European centres. The association between RRT and the primary outcome of 180-day all-cause mortality (with survival censored at heart transplantation or durable left ventricular assist device implantation) was assessed using a 1:1 propensity score-matched cohort. Factors associated with RRT were identified using multivariable logistic regression. Among 1043 patients, 972 were included, of whom 340 (35.0%) required RRT. RRT was associated with higher 180-day all-cause mortality both before (Kaplan-Meier estimates, 59.7% vs. 35.2%; HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.67-2.49; p < 0.01) and after propensity score matching (59.0% vs. 41.4%; HR 1.48, 95% CI 1.14-1.92; p < 0.01); restricted mean survival difference -25.5 days, 95% CI - 39.9 to -10.2. Factors associated with RRT included BMI ≥ 30 kg/m² (adjusted OR [aOR] 1.69; 95% CI 1.15-2.46), baseline serum creatinine (per 20 µmol/L increase: aOR 1.18; 95% CI 1.12-1.24), norepinephrine use (aOR 1.72; 95% CI 1.19-2.49), and lactate ≥4 mmol/L at implantation (aOR 1.56; 95% CI 1.11-2.20). In this large European registry of mAFP-supported CS, RRT was frequent and associated with increased 180-day mortality and greater shock severity.

papers.abstract: Cardiology consultations may be requested during preoperative anesthetic assessment before non-cardiac surgery. However, data regarding their impact on perioperative management are limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of preoperative cardiology consultations on perioperative patient management. We conducted a prospective, observational, single-center study in the Department of Anesthesiology and Critical Care at Angers University Hospital from September 1st, 2024, to August 31st, 2025. All patients referred for cardiology assessment after the anesthetic consultation were included. The primary endpoint was any change in perioperative management, including specific preoperative cardiac treatment, postponement or cancellation of surgery, and modification of anesthetic or surgical protocols. The secondary endpoint was to assess adherence of preoperative cardiac evaluation to current guideline recommendations. Among 9,621 preoperative anesthetic consultations, 138 (1%) patients were referred for cardiology assessment by the anesthesiologist and included in the study. 59 (43%) patients experienced a change in perioperative management. Of them, surgery was postponed in 52 (38%) patients, with a median delay of 81 [47-145] days, whereas only 6 patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention (angioplasty, valvuloplasty, or electrical cardioversion). A previously unknown cardiac condition was identified in 19 (15%) patients. 111 (80%) cardiology referrals were consistent with current recommendations. In our study, preoperative cardiology consultations requested by an anesthesiologist were rare but frequently responsible for modification of perioperative management. These consultations often resulted in postponement of surgery, while only a small proportion of patients underwent an invasive cardiac intervention.

papers.abstract: Many patients present for surgery soon after concussion, when cerebral physiologic regulation may remain disturbed, and no evidence-based guideline or standardized consensus recommendations exist. We sought expert consensus for adults with recent concussion undergoing noncardiac extracranial surgery. We conducted a two-round modified Delphi study (November 2025-March 2026). Round 1 items, drafted from a systematic literature search, included case vignettes. Experts identified by bibliographic screening, directories, and nomination rated items on a five-point Likert scale; "do not know" responses were excluded from the denominator. Consensus was defined a priori as 75% agreement or greater, and strong consensus as 85% or greater. Thirty-five experts (33 anesthesiologists) from 17 countries completed both rounds; 13 of 16 Round 2 statements reached consensus. Agreement was unanimous for preoperative screening for concussion symptoms and neurologic red flags, and for avoidance of hypoxemia, abnormal carbon dioxide tension, sustained hypotension, and marked hypertension. Strong consensus supported generally deferring elective surgery until concussion symptoms resolve (97%), preoperative counseling (97%), structured follow-up (94%), and extended postoperative monitoring in higher-risk patients (91%). Consensus was not reached for regional anesthesia or monitored anesthesia care over general anesthesia (74%), electroencephalography-based depth of anesthesia monitoring (73%), or cautious long-acting neuraxial opioid use (69%). The panel did not define symptom resolution and established no symptom-independent waiting interval or concussion-specific numeric physiologic threshold. This anesthesiology-led consensus supports symptom-guided timing, physiologic stability, counseling, and structured follow-up; anesthetic technique, electroencephalographic monitoring, and neuraxial opioid use remain unresolved. The statements form an expert-informed framework, not an evidence-based practice guideline.

papers.abstract: Acute pain in the postoperative period and pre-existing cognitive impairment (CI) are both independently associated with increased postoperative adverse outcomes. Pre-existing cognitive impairment may interfere with the reporting, recognition, and treatment of pain in this population. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the impact of pre-existing cognitive impairment on pain and analgesic consumption after surgery in adults. MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched for randomized controlled trials and cohort studies for adults undergoing non-cardiac, emergency, or elective surgery until April 9, 2026. Surgical patients with pre-existing cognitive impairment were compared to cognitively intact peers. The primary outcomes assessed were subjective ratings of pain and analgesic consumption postoperatively. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I and certainty of evidence was rated by GRADE. Meta-analysis used standard mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals. Thirteen studies (37,918 patients) were included. Approximately one third (33%; 95% CI 0.25-0.41) of adult surgical patients screened positive for preoperative cognitive impairment. Subjective pain scores did not differ significantly between patients with and without cognitive impairment (Hedge's g: 0.11 (SD -0.15-0.36, I2 85.3%, T2 0.073). Patients with cognitive impairment had significantly less analgesic consumption than their cognitively intact counterparts (Cohen's d: 0.53 (0.29-0.76, I2 67.4%, T2 0.028). Despite comparable pain scores, those with cognitive impairment received significantly less postoperative analgesia, raising concern for systematic under-recognition and undertreatment of pain. Increased awareness of this discrepancy and the use of standardized analgesia protocols may improve postoperative outcomes. International Registry of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO:1117357).

papers.abstract: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare pharmacogenetic condition with substantial morbidity and mortality. The current gold standard for diagnosis, caffeine-halothane contracture testing (CHCT), is invasive, costly, and available only at a single centre in Canada. Genetic testing offers a less invasive alternative, but access remains inconsistent across Canadian provinces. We sought to evaluate the cost-consequences and diagnostic wait times of a genetics-first vs biopsy-first strategy for MH susceptibility. We conducted a retrospective cost-consequence analysis of 1,208 patients referred to the Canadian Malignant Hyperthermia Investigation Unit (2015-2024) with a personal or family history suggestive of MH, and their first-degree relatives. We compared the direct, indirect, and societal costs of the Ontario genetics-first approach with those of a hypothetical biopsy-first approach used in other provinces. We analyzed diagnostic timelines using Kaplan-Meier survival analyses. In the genetics-first strategy, 7.2% of probands (88/1,208) had a diagnostic variant and did not require biopsy for contracture testing, resulting in modest societal cost reduction for probands compared with the biopsy-first strategy (CAD 23.5M vs CAD 24.3M, respectively; CAD 700 saved per proband tested). The costs of cascade testing of their first-degree relatives were three-fold lower for the genetics-first strategy (CAD 3.6M vs CAD 11.3M). The median [interquartile range] time to diagnosis was 2 [1-5] months for patients with diagnostic variants, compared with 39 [22-51] months for those requiring biopsy (log-rank P < 0.001). Compared with a hypothetical biopsy-first approach, offering genetics testing as initial step to all individuals with clinical suspicion of MH susceptibility did not increase societal costs, and resulted in substantial cost savings for cascade testing of their relatives, markedly shortening time to diagnosis for individuals who harbour a diagnostic variant.

papers.abstract: Intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) is the recommended first-line treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), particularly when cardiovascular compromise occurs. However, uncertainty persists regarding the optimal lipid formulation, specifically the comparative efficacy of ILEs containing 100% long-chain triglycerides (LCT) versus ILEs containing a 50/50 mixture of medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MCT/LCT), as well as ILEs with a 20% versus 30% lipid concentration. The primary aim of this narrative review was to compare the efficacy of 100% LCT-containing ILEs versus 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs by analyzing their respective mechanisms of action in experimental models of local anesthetic-induced cardiovascular toxicity, whereas the secondary objective was to compare ILEs with a 20% versus a 30% lipid concentration. The review also integrates the physiological rationale underlying lipid resuscitation and explores a mechanistically informed framework for interpreting formulation-specific effects of ILEs. A literature search of PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar was conducted from January 1998 through January 2026. Twenty experimental studies were identified-nine in vitro, one ex vivo, and ten in vivo-and qualitatively synthesized according to their principal mechanisms of action, including lipid shuttle, cardiotonic, vascular, and metabolic effects. The available experimental evidence suggests that 100% LCT-containing ILEs provide greater overall cardiovascular recovery than 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs, particularly through more effective lipid-shuttle activity and sustained myocardial protection. Conversely, 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs demonstrated greater vascular effects in several experimental models. Evidence comparing lipid concentrations was limited to 100% LCT-containing formulations and generally showed greater pharmacokinetic, hemodynamic, and survival effects with a 30% versus a 20% lipid concentration when administered at the same volume. The available evidence is derived exclusively from heterogeneous preclinical experimental models and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than practice-informing. Triglyceride composition and lipid concentration may influence distinct mechanisms contributing to cardiovascular recovery during LAST. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for exploring formulation-phenotype associations but do not establish formulation-specific treatment recommendations. Further experimental and translational studies are needed to determine whether these mechanistic findings translate into clinically meaningful benefits in patients with LAST.

papers.abstract: Severe neurologic injury after uncomplicated general anesthesia in previously healthy patients is rare. Since 2021, reports from South America and later from North America and Europe have described catastrophic neurologic deterioration and death after routine general anesthesia in children and adults with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. A homoplasmic mitochondrial DNA variant, MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C (p.Leu158Pro), affecting complex I of the electron transport chain, has emerged as the leading candidate susceptibility factor. This systematic review identified, appraised, and synthesized available evidence linking inhaled anesthetics, in particular sevoflurane, with severe perioperative neurologic complications in carriers of this variant and in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261471143), with searches of major biomedical databases, gray literature, and variant databases. The evidence describes a consistent but incompletely characterized syndrome defined by maternal Venezuelan ancestry, apparent preoperative health, predominant sevoflurane exposure, delayed emergence, and severe basal ganglia injury with frequent death. In patient-derived fibroblasts and cybrids, sevoflurane markedly suppressed complex I-dependent respiration, whereas propofol did not. Incidence, penetrance, and agent-specific risk remain uncertain. Cautious perioperative strategies that avoid volatile anesthetics appear justified.

papers.abstract: The present study compared the effects of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) with automated volume guarantee (HFOV-VG) versus careful manual high-frequency tidal volume (VThf) monitoring (HFOV-VM) on the incidences of hypo/hypercarbia in neonates. In this open-labeled, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, 60 neonates failing conventional mechanical ventilation were allocated to receive HFOV-VG (n = 30) versus HFOV-VM (n = 30) as a rescue mode. The primary outcome was the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia at 1 h. Secondary outcomes were incidences of hypo/hypercarbia at 6/12/24/48 h and beyond, time-specific trends for partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), delivered VThf and mean airway pressure (MAP), cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and regional cerebral oxygenation (CrSO2), duration of respiratory support, and incidences of in-hospital adverse events. Stata 18 was used for an intention-to-treat analysis. The incidence of hypo- or hypercarbia at 1 h of intervention was 15/30 (50%) in the HFOV-VG and 13/30 (43%) in the HFOV-VM groups (p = 0.61). No differences were observed in the incidences of hypo- or hypercarbia anytime during HFOV. Time-specific pCO2, VThf, and MAP were similar. On regression analysis, the only significant predictor for pCO2 at 1 h was the baseline pCO2 level in both the groups. No difference was observed in ACA-CBF, CrSO2, duration of respiratory support, and in-hospital adverse events including mortality. There was no difference in the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia with HFOV-VG versus HFOV-VM at 1 h and throughout the duration of ventilation with a similar rate of complications when used as a rescue therapy. papers.abstract: Postoperative hypotension can be caused by vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. We sought to estimate the effects of these causes on the incidence of hypotension after major vascular surgery. We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study of male and female adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery. We conducted point-of-care ultrasound and sidestream darkfield microscopy imaging to detect vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. The primary outcome was hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or a vasopressor infusion) within 24 hr of surgery. We recruited 100 patients, of whom 89 had data available for analysis. Hypotension occurred in 20 participants (23%), vasodilation in 30 (34%), and myocardial dysfunction in 11 (12%). Severe hypovolemia and obstruction were not observed. The adjusted marginal risk difference of hypotension was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 14% to 53%; P < 0.001) for vasodilation and 41% (95% CI, 3% to 79%; P = 0.03) for myocardial dysfunction. Vasodilation increased the risk of intensive care unit admission by 27% (95% CI, 8% to 45%; P = 0.006) and of requiring a vasopressor infusion by 22% (95% CI, 4% to 39%; P = 0.02). Vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction increased the risk of postoperative hypotension, providing insight into the mechanistic development of postoperative hypotension. The absence of severe hypovolemia was surprising. Clinicians should assess for vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction as potential preludes to postoperative hypotension, potentially using point-of-care echocardiography and sidestream darkfield microscopy.

papers.abstract: ARDS comprises distinct inflammatory subphenotypes, including hyper- and hypo-inflammatory forms. Whether these differ in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and response to ventilatory strategies remains unclear. Dual-energy CT enables regional assessment of aeration and perfusion. This experimental study aimed to compare V/Q mismatch between hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes, and respective responses to PEEP and prone positioning. In 10 pigs, hypo-inflammatory ARDS was induced by lung lavage followed by injurious ventilation. Hyper-inflammatory ARDS was produced by i.v. endotoxin infusion and fluid loading. Pigs were randomised to hypo- or hyperinflammatory ARDS, with similar oxygenation impairment. Dual-energy CT scans were obtained at individualised low, optimal, and high PEEP settings, in supine and prone positions. V/Q was derived from regional gas and blood volume and classified as low ( 2). Linear mixed-effects models included injury group, PEEP, and posture as fixed effects, and subject as a random effect. Hyper-inflammatory injury showed more severe V/Q mismatch than hypo-inflammatory injury (normal V/Q: 35% [sd=10] vs 51% [8] at low PEEP, supine position; P<0.01). Both PEEP optimisation and prone positioning improved V/Q. Prone positioning reduced high V/Q and dead space in hypo-inflammatory injury (group×posture interaction: F1,50=4.32, P=0.04), whereas PEEP reduced low V/Q and shunt in the supine position independent of ARDS subphenotype. In porcine models of hyper- and hypo-inflammatory ARDS, hyper-inflammatory injury was associated with more severe V/Q mismatch despite similar oxygenation. Distinct responses to PEEP and prone positioning support a subphenotype-tailored approach to ventilatory management.

papers.abstract: Canada faces mounting anesthesia workforce pressures, particularly in rural and smaller urban centres. Understanding residents' motivations regarding practice setting, research, and fellowship training is essential for workforce planning. We aimed to update a 2015 national survey to characterize current preferences and temporal shifts among Canadian anesthesiology residents. We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional survey of residents in accredited Canadian anesthesiology programs (November-December 2024) using Research Electronic Data Capture. Items addressed demographics, practice setting, research experience and intentions, and fellowship plans. Selected responses were compared with 2015 survey items using Chi square tests and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; all tests used an alpha of 0.05. Ninety-four residents responded (12% response rate). Most preferred academic practice (63%), and half preferred to remain at their training institution (49%). Interest in rural practice was reported by 49%. Although research participation was common during medical school (94%) and residency (83%), only 18% intended to pursue research after residency. Approximately 63% intended to pursue fellowship training. Compared with the 2015 survey, there were significant increases in intention to remain at the same institution (from 35% to 50%; P = 0.02) and residency research participation (from 69% to 83%; P < 0.01), whereas intention to pursue research after residency declined (from 34% to 18%; P < 0.01). Canadian anesthesiology residents continue to favour academic practice and fellowship training, yet fewer plan to integrate research into future careers. These findings highlight opportunities for targeted mentorship, greater research autonomy, financial support, and expanded rural training pathways to align resident priorities with workforce needs.

papers.abstract: The solicitation of same-day consent for participation in clinical research is commonly prohibited by research ethics boards because of concerns about limited decision-making time and patient vulnerability. However, these concerns lack empirical support and restrict both research efforts and patient participation opportunities, particularly in medical specialties such as emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesiology, in which clinicians and patients interact for the first time on the day of a procedure. We aimed to assess the voluntariness of research consent solicited on the day of surgery compared with consent obtained in advance. We performed a prospective, noninferiority randomized controlled trial examining the voluntariness of informed consent to participate in a low-risk clinical research trial at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The trial design included active deception (invitation to participate in a fabricated research trial) to capture authentic measurements of participants' perceptions of any perceived coercion. We randomized 114 patients scheduled to undergo anterior cruciate ligament repair for recruitment into a fabricated low-risk perioperative research trial at one of two time points: at a virtual preanesthesia clinic appointment in advance of the day of surgery, or on the day of surgery. Regardless of their decision, all participants received the (same) standard of care. Overall, 71/114 patients (62%) either consented to participate in the fabricated trial or declined participation but consented to a feedback session during which perceptions of coercion were assessed. Greater participation was observed among patients approached on the day of surgery (fabricated trial, 26/58 [45%]; feedback session only, 18/58 [31%]) than in advance (fabricated trial, 17/56 [30%]; feedback session only, 10/56 [18%]). Perceived coercion, measured using two validated psychometric instruments, did not differ between patients recruited on the day of surgery and those recruited in advance. A subset of patients in each group reported modest perceptions of undue influence, but regardless of recruitment time point, these patients demonstrated their agency to decline participation. Our findings suggest that restrictive same-day consent policies, when based on concerns regarding undue influence, may represent a structural barrier to participation in low-risk trials that lacks empirical justification. 1) Open Science Framework ( 46twc ); first submitted 17 March 2023; 2) ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT07380035 ); first submitted 16 January 2026.

papers.abstract: Post-ICU care often misses patients unable to attend in-person clinic visits. Remote assessments of physical function might increase access to ICU aftercare. We investigated whether patient-reported disability predicts handgrip strength (HGS) and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) distance with sufficient clinical accuracy. This secondary analysis of the stepped-wedge cluster-randomised Enhanced Recovery after Intensive Care trial included patients from 10 German ICU clusters who completed the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 plus either HGS, the 2MWT, or both, 6 months after ICU discharge. Relationships between WHODAS 2.0, HGS, and 2MWT were analysed using scatter plots, correlation coefficients, linear regressions, and Bland-Altman plots. Predictions of HGS and the 2MWT were compared with the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for both measures. Of 1463 enrolled patients, 620 were analysed. The median WHODAS 2.0 sum score was 11 (Q1, Q3: 3, 22). The median HGS, expressed as a percentage of the expected value (%exp), was 70.6%exp (Q1, Q3: 54.4, 85.6), and the median 2MWT distance was 73.7%exp (Q1, Q3: 61.5, 85.8). The 2MWT was not completed by 59% of patients. Higher disability was moderately correlated with lower HGS (Spearman %exp: -0.41) and shorter 2MWT distance (Spearman %exp: -0.47). In multivariable regression models, the WHODAS 2.0 sum score predicted HGS in kg (β: -0.27 [95% CI: -0.33 to -0.22]; P<0.001) and 2MWT distance in m (β: -1.94 [95% CI: -2.37 to -1.51]; P<0.001), but the limits of agreement exceeded the MCIDs. With increasing disability, HGS and 2MWT performance declined, although correlations were moderate and uncertainty of predictions exceeded MCIDs of both instruments. Remote WHODAS 2.0 assessments cannot replace in-person physical function testing. NCT03671447.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Interstage infants with single‐ventricle (SV) physiology following Stage I palliation represent a high‐risk population for noncardiac procedures requiring anesthesia. Data comparing perioperative outcomes by shunt type remain limited. Aims Describe anesthetic management, perioperative complications, and postoperative outcomes in interstage SV infants undergoing noncardiac interventions and compare outcomes between right ventricle‐to‐pulmonary artery (Sano) and modified Blalock‐Taussig‐Thomas shunt (mBTTS) patients. Methods We performed a retrospective single‐center cohort study of interstage SV infants with Stage I palliation undergoing noncardiac surgery or nonsurgical procedures requiring anesthesia between 2015 and 2023. Outcomes were stratified by shunt type. Results A total of 208 noncardiac interventions in 120 interstage SV infants were analyzed; 136 (65.4%) encounters in 86 Sano patients and 72 (34.6%) encounters in 34 mBTTS patients. Compared with mBTTS infants, Sano patients underwent interventions at a younger age (57 [IQR 40–83] vs. 105 [59–278] days, p < 0.001) and lower weight (3.6 [3.0–4.1] vs. 4.8 [3.4–7.3] kg, p < 0.001). mBTTS procedures had higher rates of ventricular dysfunction (34.3% vs. 12.7%, p < 0.001), chromosomal abnormalities (63.9% vs. 19.1%, p < 0.001), gastrointestinal comorbidities (87.5% vs. 72.1%, p = 0.014), and hematologic comorbidities (41.7% vs. 22.8%, p = 0.006). Hemodynamic instability requiring vasoactive support was the most common perioperative complication and occurred similarly between groups (31.9% mBTTS vs. 31.6% Sano, p = 0.962). There were no perioperative cardiac arrests. Rates of postoperative escalation of care (2.9%), reintubation (3.0% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999), readmission (16.2% vs. 16.9%, p = 0.999), and 30‐day mortality (2.3% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999) were low and comparable between groups. Conclusions Despite the high‐risk physiology of interstage SV patients, perioperative outcomes were comparable between Sano and mBTTS cohorts. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not imply low procedural risk. Favorable outcomes likely reflect careful patient selection, multidisciplinary perioperative care, and specialized institutional expertise.

papers.abstract: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is widely used for primary breast cancer surgery (BCS), though its clinical benefits within optimized multimodal analgesia pathways remain uncertain. Intravenous lidocaine infusion (IVLI) offers a simple, reproducible alternative with potential systemic analgesic effects. This randomized, tripleblinded, placebo controlled, twocentre trial compared the quality of recovery after ESPB versus IVLI for BCS. Eighty adult patients undergoing primary BCS, with or without axillary dissection, were randomized to receive either ultrasoundguided ESPB (n=40) or intraoperative IVLI (n=40), in addition to a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol. The primary outcome was quality of recovery (QoR15) score at 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, opioid consumption, adverse events, and rescue analgesia requirements. Both interventions produced excellent postoperative recovery, with 24hour QoR15 scores approaching preoperative baselines with no significant difference between groups (mean (SD) 24-hour QoR score; ESPB vs. IVLI group, 137.7(17.9) vs. 136.3(8.8), p=0.61). Pain burden and analgesic requirements over the first 24 hours were similarly low, and no ESPB or lidocainerelated adverse events were observed. Within a standardized multimodal analgesic framework, postoperative recovery and analgesic outcomes did not differ significantly between IVLI and ESPB, suggesting that IVLI may offer a pragmatic alternative when regional anesthesia expertise is limited.

papers.abstract: Recovery after non-cardiac surgery increasingly occurs at home, where clinical deterioration may go unrecognized. Digital health interventions may extend postoperative surveillance beyond discharge, but vary widely in components and clinician involvement. We evaluated their association with readmission and other outcomes. Five databases were searched from inception to December 12, 2025, for prospective randomized and observational studies comparing digital health interventions with standard care in adults after non-cardiac surgery. Readmission was the primary outcome; all-cause and major complications, emergency room (ER) visits, length of stay (LOS), and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were secondary. Interventions were grouped by whether a clinician reviewed patient-submitted data and had the ability to take action (active clinician involvement). Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RR), mean differences (MD), and standardized mean differences (SMD). p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg). In 38 studies (30 randomized, 8 observational; 7,494 patients), digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions (17 studies, n=3,944; RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73-0.99, adjusted p=0.045), ER visits (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.97), and major complications (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.94), but not all-cause complications (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79-1.08) or LOS (MD -0.04 days, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.18). Pain and anxiety were lower and functional status, quality-of-life, and satisfaction scores higher (absolute SMD 0.41-0.69). Readmission risk was lower with active clinician involvement (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64-0.92) but not without it (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78-1.18; interaction p=0.029). Heterogeneity in interventions, cohorts, and outcomes was substantial (PROM I² 50-97%). Digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions, ER visits, major complications, and better PROMs, but not fewer all-cause complications or shorter LOS. The readmission association was concentrated in studies with active clinician involvement. Heterogeneity was substantial and certainty of evidence low to very low.

papers.abstract: Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs. In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association. Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04). The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

papers.abstract: Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department. A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis. Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance. The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

papers.abstract: Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery. In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set. Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3. The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

papers.abstract: Summary Introduction Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first‐attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. Methods We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. Results During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/420, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30–2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38–7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16–0.88, p = 0.025). Discussion Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population.

papers.abstract: Heart rate (HR) and arterial blood pressure (BP) monitoring is standard of care during paediatric anaesthesia, yet evidence-based reference values for anaesthetised children remain limited. Existing BP reference values do not account for the combined effects of age, sex, weight, and height, and HR reference values in this population are lacking. We conducted a retrospective multicentre study using data from the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group anaesthesia registry (2016-22). Included patients were aged <18 yr, ASA physical status 1 or 2, and undergoing noncardiac procedures under general anaesthesia. We used quantile regression to model the 2.3rd, 16th, 50th, 84th, and 97.7th centiles for HR, mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic BP, and diastolic BP at two time points: the preparation phase (end of induction) and surgical phase (15-35 min after procedure start). Model covariates included age, sex, weight, and height. We selected the best model for each outcome using cross-validation with pinball loss. A total of 284 385 patients from 57 institutions were analysed. Optimal model complexity varied by outcome: a two-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for preparation phase HR and surgical phase MAP. A three-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for the remaining outcomes. Comprehensive prediction tables and an interactive web-based tool were developed for all outcomes. This study provides integrated HR and BP reference values for healthy paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia, incorporating age, sex, weight, and height simultaneously. These reference values with an interactive website can support clinical decision-making and haemodynamic monitoring.
